verses.text: Now the prophets, Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem. They prophesied to them in the name of the God of Israel.
Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak rose up and began to build God’s house which is at Jerusalem; and with them were the prophets of God, helping them.
At the same time Tattenai, the governor beyond the River came to them, with Shetharbozenai, and their companions, and asked them, “Who gave you a decree to build this house, and to finish this wall?”
They also asked for the names of the men were who were making this building.
But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not make them cease, until the matter should come to Darius, and an answer should be returned by letter concerning it.
The copy of the letter that Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, and Shetharbozenai, and his companions the Apharsachites, who were beyond the River, sent to Darius the king follows.
They sent a letter to him, in which was written: To Darius the king, all peace.

Be it known to the king that we went into the province of Judah, to the house of the great God, which is built with great stones, and timber is laid in the walls. This work goes on with diligence and prospers in their hands.
Then we asked those elders, and said to them thus, “Who gave you a decree to build this house, and to finish this wall?”
We asked them their names also, to inform you that we might write the names of the men who were at their head.

Thus they returned us answer, saying, “We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and are building the house that was built these many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and finished.

But after that our fathers had provoked the God of heaven to wrath, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house, and carried the people away into Babylon.
But in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king made a decree to build this house of God.

The gold and silver vessels of God’s house, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple that was in Jerusalem, and brought into the temple of Babylon, those Cyrus the king also took out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered to one whose name was Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor.
He said to him, ‘Take these vessels, go, put them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let God’s house be built in its place.’
Then the same Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of God’s house which is in Jerusalem. Since that time even until now has it been in building, and yet it is not completed.

Now therefore, if it seems good to the king, let a search be made in the king’s treasure house, which is there at Babylon, whether it is so, that a decree was made of Cyrus the king to build this house of God at Jerusalem; and let the king send his pleasure to us concerning this matter.”

footnotes.content: The prophets Haggai and Zechariah arrive at a crucial moment—when the work has stalled and fear has set in. God did not leave His people silent but sent His voice through men who had walked in exile and knew how to call a scattered flock home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When a man stands up to rebuild what has been broken, he does not stand alone—the prophets stood with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. This is how God's work moves forward: by the courage of leaders and the witness of His servants who believe before the outcome is sure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The governor's question cuts straight to authority—'Who gave you a decree?' It is the question power always asks when something unsanctioned begins to grow. But notice: the Jews do not hide or dismantle. They answer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tattenai wants names—he wants to know who to hold accountable. He does not realize he is writing down the names of the faithful, the ones who will be remembered not for defying an empire but for answering a call from beyond.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the hinge of the moment: 'The eye of their God was on the elders.' The governor cannot see what God sees. He cannot stop what God holds in His sight. When the eye of God is upon us, obstruction becomes only a letter sent upward to a king who will, in time, answer aright.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tattenai writes formally, carefully, as an administrator protecting himself. He documents what he has seen: great stones, timber in the walls, work proceeding with diligence. He sends the facts and lets the king decide, unknowing that he is simply laying the case before a ruler God has already moved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'To Darius the king, all peace.' These formal words mask Tattenai's unease. He opens the letter not in anger but in the careful tone of a man who wishes to inform rather than accuse—yet he does not know he is writing a letter that will move a king's heart to let the Jews finish what they have begun.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Listen to Tattenai's grudging admiration: the work 'goes on with diligence and prospers in their hands.' He came to obstruct but found persistence. He came skeptical but found a house rising. Sometimes our opposition becomes the very proof of what God is doing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Once more Tattenai asks: 'Who gave you a decree?' He cannot let it go because authority matters to him. But the Jews will answer calmly, knowing the decree is not held in parchment alone but in the heart of a God who remembers His covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tattenai wants names because names are currency in an empire—know the leaders, and you know where power lies. He is collecting evidence, not realizing he is recording the names of those through whom God will restore His house. In His kingdom, names matter too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth'—this is not arrogance but clarity. The elders speak plainly, claiming no authority but God's. They recall the king who built the original house, acknowledging what was lost, and in that memory plant the seed of what must be restored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The elders do not spare themselves the truth: 'Our fathers provoked the God of heaven to wrath.' They have learned that grace follows judgment, and judgment followed their rebellion. This honest reckoning is what opens the door for return—the Lord does not restore what refuses to remember its breaking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the first year of Cyrus—a Gentile king, not an Israelite—the decree comes. God's purposes move through the hearts of pagan rulers as readily as through prophets. Cyrus does not know he is fulfilling a word spoken seventy years before, yet his decree is as true as Haggai's call.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The vessels taken in plunder by Nebuchadnezzar are now released by Cyrus and entrusted to Sheshbazzar. What was stolen becomes a gift. What was scattered is gathered. This is how God restores—He takes what was broken and gives it back as a sign of covenant kept.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Let God's house be built in its place.' Cyrus speaks as though he were commanded by a power he does not name. In that moment, the will of a king aligns with the will of God—a rare and precious grace that breaks chains and opens doors.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sheshbazzar laid the foundations; then came long waiting, incomplete for years. The work stalls. The people tire. Yet in that unfinished space, God has not forgotten—He will send prophets, He will move a king, He will see it finished. Our delays are not His forgetfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this closing plea: 'Search the treasure house... and let the king send his pleasure.' How often do we wait for permission from earthly powers, not realizing the One whose eye is already upon us has already decreed our restoration? The answer from heaven comes first; the earthly confirmation follows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
